module.title: Unit 11: Food Waste & Global Food Security
module.objective: Mampu menganalisis masalah pemborosan pangan dan solusi ketahanan pangan global dengan quantifier dan adverb of degree.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Feeding the Planet Sustainably
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Food Systems, Waste Reduction, and Nutrition

content.summary: In this mission, you will explore how modern societies produce, distribute, and waste food. You will learn to identify quantifiers and adverbs of degree while reading about global food security and practical solutions to reduce waste.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Quantifiers (a lot of, plenty of, hardly any, a great deal of, too much, too many, not enough) and Adverbs of Degree (extremely, fairly, quite, slightly, absolutely)
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Food waste, food security, landfill, surplus, sustainable, malnutrition, distribution, spoil, scarcity, consume
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for numerical data and degree modifiers, and skimming to understand problem-solution structures in factual articles.

learningObjectives: Understand the main arguments in a B1 text about food waste and global hunger.
Locate specific details about how surplus food can be managed effectively.
Recognize how quantifiers and degree adverbs show quantities and emphasize key facts.

contextWarmup.prompt: What usually happens to unsold fruit and vegetables in most major grocery stores?
options: A large amount is thrown away even though it is safe to eat.
All of it is immediately delivered to families in need.
Supermarkets keep selling it until every single piece is purchased.
contextWarmup.explanation: Around the world, stores often discard surplus produce simply because items have small marks or odd shapes, creating unnecessary waste.

rules: Use 'too much' with uncountable nouns like food or waste, and 'too many' with countable plural nouns like meals or apples.
Use quantifiers like 'a great deal of' for large uncountable amounts, and 'hardly any' when an amount is close to zero.
Place adverbs of degree such as 'extremely', 'fairly', or 'quite' before adjectives or adverbs to change their strength.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use 'too many' with uncountable nouns like 'food' or 'rubbish'. Remember that 'food' is uncountable when talking about the general substance.
commonTrap.wrong: There is too many food waste rotting in local landfills.
commonTrap.correct: There is too much food waste rotting in local landfills.

grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practice affirmative, negative, and descriptive forms:

items.exampleSentence: The bakery donates surplus bread to the shelter every evening.
We must adopt sustainable habits to protect the soil for future crops.
Proper diets can prevent malnutrition among young school children.
Better transport allows a faster distribution of fresh produce to remote towns.
Milk will spoil very quickly if you leave it on the kitchen table in warm weather.
Water scarcity makes it hard for small farms to grow enough corn.
Families should try to consume fresh groceries before purchasing new ones.

paragraphs: Every year, farmers across the world grow plenty of food, but a great deal of it never reaches a family dinner table. In fact, experts estimate that nearly one-third of all agricultural produce becomes food waste. Much of this edible food rots slowly in landfills, where it releases greenhouse gases that damage the atmosphere.

At the same time, global food security remains an extremely serious problem. While shoppers in wealthy nations often buy too much food and discard surplus items simply because of small cosmetic flaws, millions of vulnerable people suffer from malnutrition. The real crisis is rarely an absolute scarcity of harvests, but rather an inefficient distribution system.

Fortunately, many communities are starting to test fairly simple solutions. A growing number of supermarkets now donate unsold items to community kitchens, and volunteers collect surplus goods before they spoil. By planning weekly meals and buying only what is necessary, ordinary citizens can make our food network much more sustainable.

questions.question: According to paragraph 1, how much agricultural produce is wasted globally?
options: Nearly one-third of all agricultural produce.
Exactly half of all food grown by farmers.
Only a tiny percentage from small local farms.
questions.answer: Nearly one-third of all agricultural produce.
questions.explanation: The text states: 'experts estimate that nearly one-third of all agricultural produce becomes food waste.'

questions.question: What happens when edible food is left to rot in landfills?
options: It produces greenhouse gases that harm the environment.
It turns directly into rich organic soil for farming.
It is collected by volunteers to feed farm animals.
questions.answer: It produces greenhouse gases that harm the environment.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that rotting food in landfills releases greenhouse gases that damage the atmosphere.

questions.question: Why do shoppers in wealthy countries often discard surplus produce?
options: Because the produce has minor cosmetic flaws.
Because the produce is completely poisonous.
Because local laws prohibit keeping leftovers.
questions.answer: Because the produce has minor cosmetic flaws.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that shoppers discard surplus items simply because of small cosmetic flaws, such as unusual shapes or marks.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the main reason why hunger still exists?
options: Food distribution is poorly organized and unequal.
The planet cannot produce enough crops for everyone.
Farmers have stopped planting basic vegetables.
questions.answer: Food distribution is poorly organized and unequal.
questions.explanation: The author notes that the problem is rarely an absolute scarcity of harvests, but rather an inefficient distribution system.

questions.question: Which quantifier in paragraph 1 describes the large amount of food that never gets eaten?
options: a great deal of
hardly any
too few
questions.explanation: The text uses 'a great deal of it never reaches a family dinner table' to describe the massive amount of wasted food.

questions.question: How does the author describe the difficulty of global food security in paragraph 2?
options: As an extremely serious problem.
As a slightly annoying routine issue.
As a problem that has already been solved.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states: 'global food security remains an extremely serious problem.'

questions.question: What action are forward-thinking supermarkets taking to reduce waste?
options: Donating unsold items to community kitchens.
Exporting discarded food to other nations.
Charging customers extra money for imperfect fruit.
questions.answer: Donating unsold items to community kitchens.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 notes that supermarkets now donate unsold items to community kitchens to help people in need.

questions.question: What role do volunteers play in community food initiatives?
options: They collect surplus goods before the items spoil.
They manage the prices of supermarket goods.
They inspect farm fields to stop crop diseases.
questions.answer: They collect surplus goods before the items spoil.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 highlights that 'volunteers collect surplus goods before they spoil.'

questions.question: How can ordinary consumers help create a more sustainable food network?
options: By planning meals and buying only what they need.
By avoiding fresh produce completely.
By dining in restaurants every evening.
questions.answer: By planning meals and buying only what they need.
questions.explanation: The text recommends 'planning weekly meals and buying only what is necessary' as an effective habit for citizens.

questions.question: What is the primary message of the reading passage?
options: Food waste can be reduced through practical community actions and better distribution.
Modern technology will soon replace traditional farming completely.
People should only purchase canned items to prevent all waste.
questions.answer: Food waste can be reduced through practical community actions and better distribution.
questions.explanation: The entire passage argues that food waste is an avoidable problem that requires fairer sharing, supermarket donations, and sensible household planning.

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear two university students, Alex and Morgan, planning a presentation on food waste and global food security. Focus on how speakers combine quantifiers and adverbs of degree to emphasize key data points and opinions. Pay close attention to connected speech features such as consonant-to-vowel linking and intrusive sounds.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic and supporting arguments regarding food waste.
Identify specific quantifiers and adverbs of degree in fast conversational English.
Notice intrusive sounds (/w/ and /j/) and consonant-vowel linking in natural speech.

keyPhrases.note: Used with uncountable nouns to show a large quantity in formal or semi-formal discussions.
Used with plural countable nouns or uncountable nouns to denote an extremely small amount.
Used with uncountable nouns to show an excessive and negative quantity.
Combines a moderating adverb of degree with an adjective to express manageable solutions.

connectedSpeech.note: The final consonant /d/ links directly into the vowel /ə/, followed by /v/ linking to /ɔː/.
When a word ending in the vowel /əʊ/ meets a following vowel, an intrusive /w/ sound smoothly bridges the gap.
The final consonant /t/ carries straight into the vowel /ɪ/ without a pause.
When a word ending in /i/ meets another vowel sound, an intrusive /j/ sound naturally appears.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Addressing Food Waste and Food Security

content.summary: Learn how to write clear, persuasive sentences about food waste and global food security. In this lesson, you will practice using quantifiers such as 'a great deal of' and 'plenty of', expressions of excess like 'too much' and 'not enough', and adverbs of degree like 'extremely' and 'fairly' to describe problems and propose practical solutions.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Quantifying Food Resources and Waste
blueprintItems.formula: Quantifier (a lot of / plenty of / hardly any / a great deal of) + Noun [Countable / Uncountable] + Verb
blueprintItems.example: A great deal of edible food ends up in rubbish bins every day.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Highlighting Excess and Scarcity
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + [too much (uncountable) / too many (countable) / not enough (both)] + Noun
blueprintItems.example: Supermarkets discard too many fresh vegetables, while low-income families do not have enough nutritious food.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Modifying Problem Severity and Solutions
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + Adverb of Degree (extremely / quite / fairly / slightly) + Adjective
blueprintItems.example: Global hunger remains an extremely serious challenge, but community food banks offer fairly simple solutions.

mechanicsRules.rule: Match your verb to the noun that follows the quantifier, not the quantifier itself.
mechanicsRules.badExample: A great deal of grain are wasted during harvest.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: A great deal of grain is wasted during harvest.
mechanicsRules.why: 'Grain' is an uncountable noun, so it requires a singular verb ('is'). Countable plural nouns like 'apples' take a plural verb ('are').

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'too much' for uncountable nouns and 'too many' for countable plural nouns.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Families throw away too many bread every week.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Families throw away too much bread every week.
mechanicsRules.why: Bread is uncountable in English. Use 'too much bread' or 'too many loaves of bread'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place a comma after an introductory dependent clause or connecting adverb at the start of a sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Although food production is high millions of people still go hungry.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Although food production is high, millions of people still go hungry.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma after the introductory clause helps the reader separate the background condition from the main clause.

sampleSentences.en: A great deal of fresh produce spoils before it reaches city markets.
sampleSentences.id: Banyak sekali hasil bumi segar membusuk sebelum sampai di pasar-pasar kota.
sampleSentences.focus: Quantifier with uncountable noun ('a great deal of fresh produce' + singular verb)

sampleSentences.en: Ordinary households waste too much food because they buy items in bulk.
sampleSentences.id: Rumah tangga biasa membuang terlalu banyak makanan karena mereka membeli barang dalam jumlah besar.

sampleSentences.en: Some poor communities have hardly any access to clean drinking water and fresh fruit.
sampleSentences.id: Beberapa komunitas miskin hampir tidak memiliki akses ke air minum bersih dan buah segar.
sampleSentences.focus: Using 'hardly any' to express severe scarcity

sampleSentences.en: The cost of transporting food across borders is extremely high.
sampleSentences.id: Biaya pengangkutan makanan lintas batas sangatlah tinggi.
sampleSentences.focus: Adverb of degree ('extremely') modifying the adjective 'high'

mechanicsChallenges.faultySentence: in many western countries too many food is thrown away every year
mechanicsChallenges.targetSentence: In many Western countries, too much food is thrown away every year.
mechanicsChallenges.translation: Di banyak negara Barat, terlalu banyak makanan dibuang setiap tahun.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Capitalize the first word and proper adjectives like 'Western', add a comma after an introductory prepositional phrase, and use 'too much' with the uncountable noun 'food'.

mechanicsChallenges.faultySentence: a great deal of farmers in sub-saharan africa does not have enough storage facilities
mechanicsChallenges.targetSentence: A great deal of farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa do not have enough storage facilities.
mechanicsChallenges.translation: Banyak sekali petani di Afrika Sub-Sahara tidak memiliki fasilitas penyimpanan yang memadai.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Capitalize proper geographical names, use the plural verb 'do not have' for the countable plural noun 'farmers', and end with a full stop.

mechanicsChallenges.faultySentence: although hunger is extremely severe some supermarkets discard plenty of unsold bread
mechanicsChallenges.targetSentence: Although hunger is extremely severe, some supermarkets discard plenty of unsold bread.
mechanicsChallenges.translation: Meskipun kelaparan sangat parah, beberapa supermarket membuang banyak roti yang tidak terjual.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Place a comma after an introductory adverbial clause and capitalize the first letter of the sentence.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Report on Household Food Waste
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences about household food waste in your area. Use at least one quantifier (such as 'plenty of' or 'a lot of') and either 'too much' or 'too many'.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Many families in my neighbourhood buy too much food during weekend sales. As a result, plenty of fresh vegetables spoil in their refrigerators. People should plan their weekly meals more carefully to avoid this problem.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Write your sentences about household food waste here...

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Solutions for Food Insecurity
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences proposing how schools or local businesses can reduce waste and help hungry people. Use at least one adverb of degree (such as 'extremely', 'fairly', or 'quite') and the phrase 'not enough'.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Many low-income families do not have enough healthy food on their tables. Local bakeries have a fairly simple way to help by donating unsold bread every evening. This approach is extremely effective when community volunteers coordinate the deliveries.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Write your proposal for community solutions here...

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence by replacing 'a lot of' with the formal quantifier 'a great deal of'.
practicumQuestions.promptText: A lot of grain spoils during transport.
targetAnswers: A great deal of grain spoils during transport.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'A great deal of' is an accurate, formal equivalent for 'a lot of' when paired with the uncountable noun 'grain'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the error in quantifier usage in the following sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Supermarkets throw away too much apples because of small bruises.
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Apples' is a countable plural noun, so use 'too many'.
targetAnswers: Supermarkets throw away too many apples because of small bruises.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Because 'apples' is a countable plural noun, you must use 'too many' rather than 'too much'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using the linking word 'although'. Place 'although' at the beginning and add appropriate punctuation.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The farm produces plenty of crops. Local families still do not have enough food.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'Although the farm produces plenty of crops,' and finish with the main clause.
targetAnswers: Although the farm produces plenty of crops, local families still do not have enough food.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When 'although' introduces a subordinate clause at the start of a sentence, a comma must follow that clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using an adverb of degree ('extremely') to make the problem sound much more urgent.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Food scarcity in dry regions is a serious concern.
targetAnswers: Food scarcity in dry regions is an extremely serious concern.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Change the article from 'a' to 'an' because 'extremely' begins with a vowel sound.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the capitalization, comma, and verb agreement errors in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: in developing nations a great deal of crops is lost after harvest
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the first letter and add a comma after the introductory phrase 'in developing nations'. 'Crops' is plural, so use 'are'.
targetAnswers: In developing nations, a great deal of crops are lost after harvest.
In developing nations, a lot of crops are lost after harvest.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The sentence begins with an introductory prepositional phrase that needs a comma, and 'crops' takes a plural verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence into the negative by replacing 'a lot of' with 'hardly any'.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The remote village has a lot of fresh produce during the winter.
practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'a lot of' with 'hardly any' to indicate that almost no fresh produce exists.
targetAnswers: The remote village has hardly any fresh produce during the winter.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Hardly any' means 'almost none' and functions as a negative quantifier without adding 'not'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Connect the two sentences using 'because' to explain the reason for the shortage.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Vulnerable families do not have enough food. Transport costs are fairly high.
practicumQuestions.hint: Join the two clauses with 'because' and do not use a comma before 'because'.
targetAnswers: Vulnerable families do not have enough food because transport costs are fairly high.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Because' introduces the cause without requiring a comma before it in standard sentence structure.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the punctuation and degree modifier mistake in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The new community garden is absolute successful in feeding hungry children
practicumQuestions.hint: Change the adjective 'absolute' to the adverb of degree 'absolutely', and add a full stop.
targetAnswers: The new community garden is absolutely successful in feeding hungry children.
The new community garden is extremely successful in feeding hungry children.
practicumQuestions.explanation: An adjective like 'successful' must be modified by an adverb of degree such as 'absolutely'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the sentence to express insufficiency by using 'not enough'.
practicumQuestions.promptText: There is too little clean water for the crops.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'There is not enough clean water for the crops.' or 'There isn't enough clean water for the crops.'
targetAnswers: There is not enough clean water for the crops.
There isn't enough clean water for the crops.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Not enough' directly replaces 'too little' to describe insufficient resources.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence by explaining how consumers can avoid buying too much food. Write one complete clause starting with 'by'.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Shoppers can reduce kitchen waste by
practicumQuestions.hint: For example: 'making a shopping list before visiting the market.'
targetAnswers: Shoppers can reduce kitchen waste by making a shopping list before visiting the market.
Shoppers can reduce kitchen waste by planning their meals in advance.
Shoppers can reduce kitchen waste by checking their pantry before they shop.
Shoppers can reduce kitchen waste by planning their meals before going to the supermarket.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a prepositional phrase with the gerund 'by + verb-ing' to describe an action that solves the problem.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Food Waste and Global Security

content.summary: In this lab, you will practice speaking clearly about food waste, sustainable farming, and global food security. You will learn how to emphasize quantifiers and adverbs of degree to express precise amounts and intensity in natural speech.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on pausing naturally between sense groups. When using degree adverbs like 'extremely' or 'far too', give them extra pitch height and volume to make your point sound convincing. Keep unstressed syllables short and clear.

pillars.name: Degree Adverb Emphasis
pillars.explanation: Put stronger emphasis on words like 'extremely', 'terribly', and 'totally' before descriptive words, for example in 'extremely wasteful' and 'terribly urgent'.

pillars.name: Quantifier Rhythm
pillars.explanation: Group quantifiers like 'a huge amount of' and 'plenty of' into one smooth speech unit rather than breaking them word by word.

pillars.name: Syllable Stress Shifts
pillars.target: Accurate stress placement on core derivatives
pillars.explanation: Notice how the stressed syllable changes or stays steady across related forms such as 'sustain' and 'sustainable', or 'distribute' and 'distribution'.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The primary stress remains on the second syllable when adding the adjective ending -able.
The main stress stays on the syllable 'cur' in both root word and noun form.
When used as a noun meaning farm crops, stress is on the first syllable. When used as an action verb, stress shifts to the second syllable.
The primary stress shifts from the second syllable to the third syllable right before the ending -tion.

drills.targetText: A huge amount of edible food ends up in landfills every single day.
drills.phonetic: /ə hjuːdʒ əˈmaʊnt əv ˈedɪbl fuːd endz ʌp ɪn ˈlændfɪlz ˈevri ˈsɪŋɡl deɪ/
drills.focus: Quantifier link 'amount of' and compound noun 'landfills'

drills.targetText: Local charities collect surplus groceries and give them to families in need.
drills.phonetic: /ˈləʊkl ˈtʃærətiz kəˈlekt ˈsɜːpləs ˈɡrəʊsəriz ænd ɡɪv ðəm tuː ˈfæməlɪz ɪn niːd/
drills.focus: Initial stress on 'surplus' and smooth rhythm
drills.hint: Keep 'surplus' stressed on the first syllable: SUR-plus.

drills.targetText: Severe malnutrition remains an extremely serious problem in dry regions.
drills.phonetic: /sɪˈvɪə ˌmælnjuːˈtrɪʃn rɪˈmeɪnz ən ɪkˈstriːmli ˈsɪəriəs ˈprɒbləm ɪn draɪ ˈriːdʒənz/
drills.focus: Stress on 'malnutrition' and adverb emphasis on 'extremely'
drills.hint: Raise pitch slightly on the second syllable of 'ex-TREME-ly'.

drills.targetText: Farmers need far more sustainable methods to secure enough food for the future.
drills.phonetic: /ˈfɑːməz niːd fɑː mɔː səˈsteɪnəbl ˈmeθədz tuː sɪˈkjʊər ɪˈnʌf fuːd fɔː ðə ˈfjuːtʃə/
drills.focus: Degree phrase 'far more' and stress on 'sustainable'
drills.hint: Elongate 'far more' before landing firmly on 'sus-TAIN-a-ble'.

roleplay.context: You are talking to Tariq, an environmental officer at your school, about reducing lunch plate waste in the canteen.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: Have you noticed how much uneaten rice and vegetables students throw away every afternoon?
turns.translation: Apakah kamu memperhatikan berapa banyak nasi dan sayur sisa yang dibuang siswa setiap siang?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Yes, an enormous amount of lunch goes straight into the trash, which is terribly wasteful.
turns.translation: Ya, sangat banyak makanan siang langsung masuk ke tempat sampah, yang sangat boros.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: What simple step can we introduce next week to keep this food out of the landfill?
turns.translation: Langkah sederhana apa yang bisa kita perkenalkan minggu depan untuk mencegah makanan ini masuk TPA?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: We can offer flexible portion sizes and create a compost bin for leftovers.
turns.translation: Kita bisa menawarkan pilihan ukuran porsi dan membuat tempat kompos untuk sisa makanan.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 25 seconds about food waste habits in your home and how your family prevents throwing away good food.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe what happens to leftover food in your house and one habit your family uses to minimize food waste.
storyPoints: What kind of food gets left over most often in your household
A practical routine your family uses to store or reuse leftovers
How this habit helps save money and reduce waste sent to landfills
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: At home we store leftover stew in the fridge and plan weekly meals so that very little food ends up in landfills.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /æt həʊm wiː stɔː ˈleftˌəʊvə stjuː ɪn ðə frɪdʒ ænd plæn ˈwiːkli miːlz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Give specific examples of food items and use quantifiers like 'very little' or 'plenty of'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 25 seconds explaining how surplus food from grocery stores can help tackle local hunger.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell a short story about a community initiative or supermarket that shares extra food with people who need it.
storyPoints: Why supermarkets often end up with a large surplus of fresh items
How local volunteers collect and deliver the extra meals
The positive result this brings to families facing malnutrition
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Supermarkets often collect surplus bread and vegetables so charities can distribute them to families suffering from malnutrition.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈsuːpəmɑːkɪts ˈɒfn kəˈlekt ˈsɜːpləs bred ænd ˈvedʒtəblz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Connect the problem of unsold surplus goods to the social benefit of reducing hunger.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are speaking with a local bakery owner about collecting unsold loaves of bread at closing time.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond to the bakery owner by proposing a practical collection routine for surplus bread.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: We bake fresh loaves every morning, but we throw away fifteen loaves at nine o'clock. What do you plan to do with them?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Our student club can collect your surplus bread every evening and deliver it immediately to a neighborhood shelter.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈaʊə ˈstjuːdnt klʌb kæn kəˈlekt jɔː ˈsɜːpləs bred ˈevri ˈiːvnɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Speak politely and clearly propose a concrete schedule and destination for the food.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A community worker asks for your opinion on solving malnutrition in nearby rural villages.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Answer the worker by recommending sustainable farming and nutritious crops.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Many young children in the outer villages face serious malnutrition. What practical project should our clinic support first?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We should support sustainable vegetable gardens so families can produce a steady supply of nutritious greens.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use the word 'sustainable' with proper syllable stress and offer a constructive agricultural answer.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your roommate bought too much fresh fruit and vegetables, and some items are already rotting in the crisper.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Address your roommate politely and propose a shared shopping list to avoid throwing food into the landfill.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: I bought all these apples and tomatoes on sale, but I guess we cannot finish them before they spoil. Should I toss them out?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Let us make a sauce tonight with the soft tomatoes so we do not send good food to the landfill.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /let ʌs meɪk ə sɔːs təˈnaɪt wɪð ðə sɒft təˈmɑːtəʊz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a cooperative tone and suggest an immediate cooking solution rather than throwing food away.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: An agricultural student asks how modern technology improves long-term food security in your country.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Explain how smart water systems and weather forecasts help protect harvest yields.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Why is everyone talking about food security this semester? Does new technology really make a difference for small farms?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, modern irrigation helps farmers grow crops through dry seasons, which is vital for national food security.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /jes ˈmɒdn ˌɪrɪˈɡeɪʃn helps ˈfɑːməz ɡrəʊ krɒps/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Deliver a well structured opinion using degree modifiers like 'vital for' and clear vocabulary.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the sentence aloud, pronouncing the core vocabulary items 'surplus' and 'landfill' with crisp articulation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Repeat this sentence clearly: Supermarkets should never dump usable surplus inventory into an open landfill.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Supermarkets should never dump usable surplus inventory into an open landfill.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈsuːpəmɑːkɪts ʃʊd ˈnevə dʌmp ˈjuːzəbl ˈsɜːpləs ˈɪnvəntri ˈɪntuː ən ˈəʊpən ˈlændfɪl/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Make sure 'surplus' has stress on the first syllable (/ˈsɜːpləs/) and 'landfill' ends with a clean dark /l/ sound.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the sentence aloud, placing appropriate vocal weight on the degree adverb 'substantially' and quantifier 'a huge amount of'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say the sentence aloud: We can substantially reduce hunger if we stop throwing away a huge amount of fresh food.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We can substantially reduce hunger if we stop throwing away a huge amount of fresh food.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wiː kæn səbˈstænʃəli rɪˈdjuːs ˈhʌŋɡə ɪf wiː stɒp ˈθrəʊɪŋ əˈweɪ ə hjuːdʒ əˈmaʊnt əv freʃ fuːd/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the adverb 'substantially' to signal degree, and link 'a huge amount of' together naturally.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice correct syllable stress on 'sus-TAIN-a-ble' and 'mal-nu-TRI-tion'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Pronounce this sentence accurately: Developing sustainable agriculture is essential to end severe malnutrition.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Developing sustainable agriculture is essential to end severe malnutrition.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /dɪˈveləpɪŋ səˈsteɪnəbl ˈæɡrɪkʌltʃər ɪz ɪˈsenʃl tuː end sɪˈvɪə ˌmælnjuːˈtrɪʃn/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Hit the primary stress on the second syllable of 'sus-TAIN-a-ble' and the third syllable of 'mal-nu-TRI-tion'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the list with rising intonation on the first two items and a definite falling tone on the final item.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this sentence with list intonation: To protect food security, we must improve storage, prevent crop diseases, and cut consumer waste.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: To protect food security, we must improve storage, prevent crop diseases, and cut consumer waste.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /tuː prəˈtekt fuːd sɪˈkjʊərəti wiː mʌst ɪmˈpruːv ˈstɔːrɪdʒ prɪˈvent krɒp dɪˈziːzɪz ænd kʌt kənˈsjuːmə weɪst/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a slight pitch rise after 'storage' and 'diseases', then finish with a clear falling tone on 'waste'.
